title: Birds: Anatomy, Behavior, and Field Identification
description: An introduction to the biology of birds for learners with no formal background. The course moves from what makes a bird a bird (feathers, skeleton and evolutionary history) through flight, internal anatomy and the senses, to the practical skill of identifying birds by sight and sound. Later chapters cover breeding, migration and the conservation of bird populations. Each chapter pairs reading with practice you can do outdoors or with photographs and recordings.
objectives: Describe the anatomical traits that define birds and explain how they support flight.
Explain the evidence that birds are living dinosaurs.
Identify common birds to species using shape, field marks, behavior, habitat and sound.
Describe how birds court, nest, raise young and migrate.
Interpret bird population data and explain the main threats to birds and the measures that have reversed declines.
Collect and submit a standardized bird survey to a citizen-science project.

title: Game Design: Systems, Mechanics, and Player Experience
description: A course for learners who have played games critically and perhaps made small prototypes, and now want the working methods of professional designers. It treats a game as a system of rules that produces player experience, and teaches the tools designers use to shape that system: core loops, feedback, economies, difficulty curves, level layout and playtesting. Every chapter ends with a design exercise that you can complete on paper or in a simple prototype.
prerequisites: Regular, attentive experience playing games in several genres
Basic arithmetic and spreadsheets; no programming required
objectives: Analyze a game in terms of mechanics, dynamics and aesthetics.
Design and diagram a core loop and its feedback systems.
Balance a small game economy using a spreadsheet model.
Plan a difficulty and pacing curve and lay out a level that teaches through play.
Run a playtest, collect usable evidence and turn it into design changes.
Write a concise design document for an original game concept.

title: Outer Space from the Ground Up
description: A first look at space for someone starting from zero. The course begins with what you can see from your own backyard and works outward: the Moon and planets, the Sun, the stars, and the galaxies beyond. Distances and sizes are built up with everyday comparisons before any numbers are introduced. You will finish able to find major objects in the night sky and explain how astronomers know what they know.
objectives: Find the Moon’s phase, at least two planets and three bright stars or constellations in the night sky.
Explain day, night, seasons and lunar phases using models you can make at home.
Describe the planets of the solar system and how they differ.
Explain what stars are and how they live and die, in plain language.
Describe the scale of the universe using comparisons and light-travel time.

title: Energy Systems: Conversion, Storage, and the Electric Grid
department: Department of Mechanical and Electrical Engineering
description: An upper-division treatment of how societies convert, store, move and use energy. The course applies thermodynamics, electrical engineering and economics to real systems: thermal power plants, wind and solar generation, batteries and other storage, and the operation of the power grid. Students work with quantitative models throughout, including efficiency limits, capacity factors, levelized cost and dispatch. The final chapter combines these tools to evaluate decarbonization pathways.
objectives: Apply the first and second laws of thermodynamics to compute efficiency limits of heat engines and real power cycles.
Analyze AC power, phasors, transmission losses and power factor in grid components.
Estimate output and capacity factor of wind and solar installations from resource data.
Compare storage technologies by energy density, power density, round-trip efficiency and cost.
Compute levelized cost of energy and explain its limits as a comparison tool.
Model merit-order dispatch and explain how variable renewables change grid operation.
